name: Physics
topics: Motion: speed, velocity, acceleration and equations of motion
Gravitational field and simple harmonic motion

questions.q: Which of the following physical quantities is a fundamental (base) quantity in the International System of Units (SI)?
questions.e: Mass is one of the seven base quantities in SI (the others are length, time, temperature, electric current, amount of substance and luminous intensity). Force, velocity and pressure are all derived from combinations of these base quantities.
questions.p: Mass na one of di seven base quantity for SI system. Force, velocity and pressure dem come from combining base quantities, so dem no be fundamental.

questions.q: A substance has mass M and occupies a volume V. In terms of the dimensions of mass (M) and length (L), what is the dimension of the density of the substance?
questions.e: Density = mass/volume = M/L³, which is written as ML⁻³. Since no time quantity is involved in density, T does not appear in its dimension.
questions.p: Density na mass divide by volume, wey be M/L³, so im dimension na ML⁻³. Time no dey involved for density, so T no go show for am.

questions.q: A motorist drives a car at a constant speed of 54 km/h along the Lagos-Ibadan expressway. What is this speed expressed in metres per second (m/s)?
questions.e: To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 1000/3600 (or divide by 3.6). So 54 x 1000/3600 = 15 m/s.
questions.p: To change km/h go m/s, multiply by 1000/3600 (or divide by 3.6). So 54 x 1000/3600 = 15 m/s.

questions.q: In an experiment to measure the diameter of a thin copper wire, a student uses a micrometer screw gauge. The main scale reading is 4.5 mm, while the thimble (circular) scale reading is 28 divisions, where each division represents 0.01 mm. What is the diameter of the wire?
questions.e: Diameter = main scale reading + (thimble reading x least count) = 4.5 mm + (28 x 0.01 mm) = 4.5 mm + 0.28 mm = 4.78 mm.
questions.p: Diameter = main scale reading add (thimble reading times least count) = 4.5mm + (28 x 0.01mm) = 4.78mm.

questions.q: The speed v of a transverse wave travelling along a stretched string depends on the tension F in the string, with dimension MLT⁻², and the mass per unit length mu of the string, with dimension ML⁻¹. Using dimensional analysis, which expression correctly gives the dimension of speed?
questions.e: Dividing F by mu gives (MLT⁻²)/(ML⁻¹) = L²T⁻², which is the dimension of speed squared, not speed. Taking the square root gives LT⁻¹, which is the correct dimension for speed, so v = √(F/mu) is dimensionally consistent.
questions.p: If you divide F by mu you go get L²T⁻², wey be speed squared, no be speed. Take square root make e come be LT⁻¹, wey be di correct dimension for speed.

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly defines a scalar quantity?
o: A quantity that has magnitude only, with no direction
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction
A quantity that is always added using the parallelogram law
A quantity whose value changes when its direction changes
questions.e: A scalar quantity is described completely by its magnitude (size) alone, with no direction attached, e.g. mass, time, and speed. Options B, C and D all describe properties of vector quantities, not scalars.
questions.p: Scalar na quantity wey get size (magnitude) only, e no get direction at all. Examples be mass, time and speed. The other options dey talk about vector wey get direction too.

questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.e: Displacement has both magnitude and a specific direction (e.g. 10 m east), making it a vector. Mass, energy and time are scalar quantities because they only have magnitude.
questions.p: Displacement na vector because e get both size and direction (e dey tell you where the object end up). Mass, energy and time na scalar quantities, dem no get direction.

questions.q: Two forces of magnitude 3 N and 4 N act on a particle such that they are perpendicular to each other. Calculate the magnitude of their resultant force.
questions.e: Since the two forces are perpendicular, Pythagoras' theorem applies: Resultant = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 N. Simply adding or subtracting the forces (giving 7 N or 1 N) is wrong because they do not act along the same line.
questions.p: Since the two forces dey perpendicular (90 degrees to each other), we go use Pythagoras theorem: Resultant = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5N. If you just add (7N) or subtract (1N) the forces, e no correct because dem no dey for same line.

questions.q: Chinedu walks 8 m due east and then 6 m due north. Calculate the magnitude of his total displacement from his starting point.
questions.e: East and north are perpendicular directions, so Pythagoras' theorem gives the displacement: √(8² + 6²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10 m. Adding the distances directly (14 m) ignores the fact that they are vectors in different directions.
questions.p: East and north dey perpendicular to each other, so we use Pythagoras: √(8² + 6²) = √(64+36) = √100 = 10m. If you just add the two distances (14m), e wrong because na vector quantities wey dey different direction.

questions.q: A force of 20 N acts on an object at an angle of 30 degrees above the horizontal. Using cos30 = √3/2 and sin30 = 1/2, calculate the magnitude of the horizontal component of this force.
questions.e: The horizontal component of a force is given by F cos(theta) = 20 x cos30 = 20 x (√3/2) = 10sqrt(3), which is about 17.3 N. Using sin30 instead of cos30 wrongly gives 10.0 N, which is actually the vertical component.
questions.p: Horizontal component na F cos(theta) = 20 x cos30 = 20 x (√3/2) = 10sqrt(3), wey be like 17.3N. If you mistakenly use sin30 you go get 10.0N, but na vertical component be that one.

questions.q: Three forces, P, Q and R, act on a point object and keep it in equilibrium. Which statement correctly describes the vector relationship between these three forces?
o: The three forces must all act along the same straight line
The sum P + Q + R, when drawn head-to-tail, must always point due north
The three forces must all have exactly equal magnitudes
When drawn head-to-tail in order, P, Q and R form a closed triangle
questions.e: For an object in equilibrium under three forces, the vector sum of the forces is zero. This means that when the force vectors are drawn head-to-tail (one after another), they form a closed triangle, with no gap left between the start of the first vector and the end of the last. Equal magnitudes or acting on one straight line are not required.
questions.p: If object dey for equilibrium under three forces, e mean say the total (vector sum) of the forces na zero. So if you draw the vectors head-to-tail one after the other, dem go close up well-well make closed triangle. The forces no need to get equal size or dey same straight line.

questions.q: A danfo bus travels a distance of 150 km in 3 hours at a constant speed. Calculate the speed of the bus.
questions.e: Speed = distance / time = 150 km / 3 h = 50 km/h.
questions.p: Speed na distance divide by time: 150 km divide by 3 h = 50 km/h.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines velocity of a moving body?
o: rate of change of speed with time
rate of change of displacement with time
rate of change of distance with time
rate of change of acceleration with time
questions.e: Velocity is a vector quantity defined as the rate of change of displacement (distance in a specified direction) with time, unlike speed which only considers distance.
questions.p: Velocity na how fast displacement (distance with direction) dey change with time, e get direction unlike speed.

questions.q: Chidi drives from Enugu to Onitsha, a distance of 120 km, in 2 hours. He returns to Enugu along the same route in 3 hours. Calculate his average speed for the whole journey.
questions.e: Total distance = 120 km + 120 km = 240 km, total time = 2 h + 3 h = 5 h. Average speed = total distance / total time = 240/5 = 48 km/h.
questions.p: Total distance na 240 km, total time na 5 hours, so average speed = 240/5 = 48 km/h.

questions.q: A motorcycle increases its velocity uniformly from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.
questions.e: Acceleration a = (v - u)/t = (25 - 5)/4 = 20/4 = 5 m/s².
questions.p: Acceleration = (v minus u) divide by time = (25-5)/4 = 5 m/s².

questions.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 10 seconds. Calculate the distance it covers in this time.
questions.e: Using s = ut + (1/2)at² with u = 0, a = 2 m/s², t = 10 s: s = 0 + 0.5 x 2 x 10² = 100 m.
questions.p: Use s = ut + 1/2 at², since u = 0: s = 0.5 x 2 x 10² = 100 m.

questions.q: A football is kicked vertically upward with an initial velocity of 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, calculate the maximum height reached by the ball.
questions.e: At maximum height, final velocity v = 0. Using v² = u² - 2gh: 0 = 20² - 2(10)h, so 20h = 400, giving h = 20 m.
questions.p: For the highest point, v = 0. From v² = u² - 2gh: 0 = 400 - 20h, so h = 400/20 = 20 m.

questions.q: A net force of 15 N acts on a block of mass 3 kg resting on a smooth table. Calculate the acceleration produced in the block.
questions.e: By Newton's second law, F = ma, so a = F/m = 15/3 = 5 m/s².
questions.p: Newton second law tell us say F = ma, so a = F/m = 15/3 = 5 m/s².

questions.q: A delivery truck of mass 1200 kg moves along the Lagos-Ibadan expressway with a velocity of 10 m/s. Calculate the momentum of the truck.
questions.e: Momentum = mass x velocity = 1200 kg x 10 m/s = 12000 kg m/s.
questions.p: Momentum = mass x velocity = 1200 kg x 10 m/s = 12000 kg m/s.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on with a stationary 4 kg ball. After collision, the two balls stick together and move with a common velocity. Calculate this common velocity.
questions.e: By conservation of momentum: m1u1 + m2u2 = (m1+m2)v, so (2x6 + 4x0) = (2+4)v, giving 12 = 6v, so v = 2 m/s.
questions.p: Momentum conservation: m1u1 + m2u2 = (m1+m2)v, so (2x6 + 4x0) = (2+4)v, e mean 12 = 6v, so v = 2 m/s.

questions.q: A hunter's gun of mass 4 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.02 kg. The bullet leaves the gun with a speed of 400 m/s. If the gun and bullet were both at rest before firing, calculate the magnitude of the recoil velocity of the gun.
questions.e: Total momentum before firing is zero, so momentum of bullet equals momentum of gun in the opposite direction: 0.02 x 400 = 4 x v, giving v = 8/4 = 2 m/s.
questions.p: Before dem shoot, total momentum na zero, so bullet momentum go equal gun momentum for opposite direction: 0.02 x 400 = 4 x v, so v = 8/4 = 2 m/s.

questions.q: In Physics, work is said to be done on an object when:
o: a force is applied to the object but the object does not move at all
a force moves the object through a distance in the direction of the force
a force acts on the object for a very long time without moving it
the object moves at constant velocity with no force acting on it
questions.e: Work is only done when a force causes an object to move through some distance in the direction of the force. If there is no displacement, no work is done, no matter how long or how hard the force is applied.
questions.p: Work dey happen only when force cause object to move for some distance for the direction wey the force dey push am. If the object no move, no work dey done, even if you push am tire.

questions.q: Chidi pushes a wooden crate along a level floor in his shop with a steady horizontal force of 40 N, moving it through a distance of 5 m. Calculate the work done by Chidi on the crate.
questions.e: Work done = Force x distance = 40 N x 5 m = 200 J. The other options come from wrongly adding or dividing the numbers instead of multiplying.
questions.p: Work wey e do = Force x distance = 40 N x 5 m = 200 J. The other answers na from wrong add or divide instead of multiply.

questions.q: A bicycle and its rider have a total mass of 15 kg and are moving at a speed of 4 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy of the bicycle and rider.
questions.e: Kinetic energy = (1/2) x mass x velocity² = 0.5 x 15 x 4² = 0.5 x 15 x 16 = 120 J. Forgetting to square the velocity or the factor of 1/2 gives the wrong options.
questions.p: Kinetic energy = (1/2) x mass x velocity² = 0.5 x 15 x 16 = 120 J. If you forget to square the speed or forget the 1/2, you go land for the wrong answers.

questions.q: A ripe mango of mass 0.5 kg hangs on a tree at a height of 8 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the potential energy of the mango relative to the ground.
questions.e: Potential energy = mgh = 0.5 kg x 10 m/s² x 8 m = 40 J. The wrong options come from using g = 1, forgetting a zero, or doubling the mass by mistake.
questions.p: Potential energy = mgh = 0.5 x 10 x 8 = 40 J. The wrong ones dey happen if you use g = 1, forget zero, or double the mass by mistake.

questions.q: A stone of mass 2 kg is released from rest and falls freely from a height of 20 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, use the principle of conservation of energy to find the speed of the stone just before it hits the ground.
questions.e: By conservation of energy, loss in potential energy equals gain in kinetic energy: mgh = (1/2)mv², so v = √2gh = √(2 x 10 x 20) = √400 = 20 m/s. Mass cancels out, so it is not needed in the final calculation.
questions.p: Energy wey the stone lose for height go turn to kinetic energy: mgh = (1/2)mv², so v = √2gh = √2x10x20 = √400 = 20 m/s. Mass cancel out, e no dey needed again for the final answer.

questions.q: In the study of simple machines, the mechanical advantage (MA) of a machine is defined as the ratio of:
o: distance moved by effort to distance moved by load
questions.e: Mechanical advantage tells us how many times a machine multiplies the effort. It is defined as Load divided by Effort (MA = Load/Effort).
questions.p: Mechanical advantage na how machine dey multiply the effort wey you put. E be Load divide by Effort (MA = Load/Effort).

questions.q: A carpenter in Aba uses an inclined plane of length 5 m to push a load up to a platform of height 1.25 m. Calculate the velocity ratio of the inclined plane.
questions.e: For an inclined plane, velocity ratio VR = length of plane / height of plane = 5/1.25 = 4. This means the effort moves 4 times the distance the load moves.
questions.p: For inclined plane, VR = length / height = 5/1.25 = 4. E mean say the effort go waka 4 times wetin the load waka.

questions.q: A simple machine has a mechanical advantage of 5 and a velocity ratio of 8. Calculate the efficiency of the machine.
questions.e: Efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100% = (5/8) x 100% = 62.5%. This shows the machine is not perfectly efficient because of friction losses.
questions.p: Efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100% = (5/8) x 100% = 62.5%. E show say the machine no reach 100% because of friction wey dey waste energy.

questions.q: A block-and-tackle pulley system is arranged with 2 pulleys fixed to the upper beam and 2 pulleys attached to the movable lower block carrying the load, making a total of 4 pulleys in the system. Assuming the rope is pulled vertically downward, what is the velocity ratio of this system?
questions.e: For a block-and-tackle system, the velocity ratio equals the number of strings (pulleys) supporting the load. With 4 pulleys sharing the load, VR = 4.
questions.p: For block-and-tackle system, VR na the number of pulley wey dey carry the load. Since 4 pulleys dey share the load, VR = 4.

questions.q: A wheel and axle machine has a wheel of radius 30 cm and an axle of radius 5 cm. If the machine is used to lift a load of 600 N and the efficiency of the machine is 80%, calculate the effort required.
questions.e: VR = R/r = 30/5 = 6. Since efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100%, MA = 0.8 x 6 = 4.8. Effort = Load/MA = 600/4.8 = 125 N.
questions.p: VR = R/r = 30/5 = 6. Since efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100%, MA = 0.8 x 6 = 4.8. Effort = Load/MA = 600/4.8 = 125 N.

questions.q: A uniform lever (class one lever) has its fulcrum between the load and effort. A load of 300 N is placed 20 cm from the fulcrum, while the effort is applied 80 cm from the fulcrum on the other side. Ignoring the weight of the lever and friction, calculate the effort needed to balance the load.
questions.e: By the principle of moments, Effort x distance from fulcrum = Load x distance from fulcrum. So Effort x 80 = 300 x 20, giving Effort = 6000/80 = 75 N.
questions.p: Using principle of moments, Effort x distance = Load x distance. So Effort x 80 = 300 x 20, e give Effort = 6000/80 = 75 N.

questions.q: Alhaji Musa pushes a heavy wooden crate across a cemented floor at Kano market. The force that opposes the relative sliding motion between the crate and the floor is called
questions.e: Friction is the force that opposes relative motion or the tendency of motion between two surfaces in contact. It acts along the surface, opposite to the direction of sliding.
questions.p: Friction na di force wey dey oppose as surface dey slide for anoda surface. Na im dey slow di crate down for ground.

questions.q: A wooden block of mass 4 kg rests on a horizontal bench. A horizontal force of 12 N is just enough to make the block start to slide. Taking g = 10 m/s², what is the coefficient of friction between the block and the bench?
questions.e: Limiting friction F = μmg. So μ = F/(mg) = 12/(4 x 10) = 12/40 = 0.3.

questions.q: A technician uses a spanner to tighten a bolt. He applies a force of 50 N perpendicular to the spanner at a distance of 0.2 m from the bolt. What is the moment of the force about the bolt?
questions.e: Moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot = 50 N x 0.2 m = 10 N m.
questions.p: Moment = force x distance wey dey perpendicular from di pivot = 50 N x 0.2 m = 10 N m.

questions.q: A uniform plank of length 4 m is balanced on a pivot placed exactly at its centre. A boy of weight 300 N sits at a point 1.5 m from the pivot on one side. At what distance from the pivot, on the other side, must a girl of weight 250 N sit for the plank to balance?
questions.e: By the principle of moments, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment: 300 x 1.5 = 250 x d, so d = 450/250 = 1.8 m.
questions.p: Dem use principle of moments: 300 x 1.5 = 250 x d, so d = 450/250 = 1.8 m.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a necessary condition for a rigid body acted upon by several coplanar forces to be in equilibrium?
o: The body must be completely at rest
The sum of clockwise moments about any point must equal the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point
The sum of the forces in any chosen direction must be zero
The sum of the forces perpendicular to any chosen direction must also be zero
questions.e: A body can be in equilibrium while moving with constant velocity (dynamic equilibrium), so it need not be at rest. The true conditions are that the resultant force and resultant moment about any point are both zero.
questions.p: Body fit dey equilibrium even if e dey move with constant speed, so e no need to dey rest. Wetin must happen na say total force and total moment for any point must be zero.

questions.q: A uniform metre rule of weight 1.0 N is freely pivoted (balanced) at the 40 cm mark. A load of 3.0 N is hung at the 10 cm mark. The weight of the rule acts at its centre, the 50 cm mark. Calculate the position (in cm from the zero end) where a force of 2.0 N must be applied, on the side away from the load, to keep the rule in equilibrium.
questions.e: Anticlockwise moment from the load = 3.0 x (40-10) = 90 N cm. Clockwise moment from the rule's weight = 1.0 x (50-40) = 10 N cm. The 2.0 N force must supply the remaining 80 N cm clockwise, so its distance from the pivot = 80/2 = 40 cm, giving a position of 40 + 40 = 80 cm from the zero end.
questions.p: Anticlockwise moment from load = 3.0 x (40-10) = 90 N cm. Clockwise moment from rule weight = 1.0 x (50-40) = 10 N cm. Di 2.0 N force need to balance di remaining 80 N cm, so e distance from pivot = 80/2 = 40 cm, e go land for 40 + 40 = 80 cm mark.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a projectile in Physics?
o: An object that moves along a circular path with a constant centripetal force
An object that moves in a straight line at constant speed under no external force
An object that is given an initial velocity and thereafter moves only under the action of gravity
An object that remains stationary while subjected to gravitational force
questions.e: A projectile is any object launched into the air that is then acted upon only by gravity (ignoring air resistance). It follows a curved path called a trajectory.
questions.p: Projectile na any object wey dem throw go air, after that na only gravity dey work on am (we no dey count air resistance). E dey follow curve path wey dem call trajectory.

questions.q: Chidi throws a stone horizontally from the top of a cliff that is 45 m high, with an initial speed of 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the time it takes the stone to reach the ground.
questions.e: For horizontal projection, vertical motion only depends on height and gravity: h = (1/2)g t². So 45 = (1/2)(10)t², giving t² = 9, t = 3.0 s. The horizontal speed does not affect the time of fall.
questions.p: For horizontal throw, na only height and gravity dey control how e take fall: h = (1/2)g t². So 45 = (1/2)(10)t², t² = 9, t = 3.0 s. The horizontal speed no dey change the time wey e go take land.

questions.q: A ball is projected from level ground with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 45° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the horizontal range of the ball.
questions.e: Range formula: R = u² sin(2theta)/g = (20²)(sin90)/10 = 400(1)/10 = 40 m. At 45°, sin(2theta)=sin90=1, giving maximum range for that speed.
questions.p: Range formula na R = u² sin(2theta)/g = (20²)(sin90)/10 = 400(1)/10 = 40 m. Since e be 45°, sin(2theta) = sin90 = 1, so the range reach im maximum for that speed.

questions.q: A car of mass 800 kg moves round a circular track of radius 50 m at a constant speed of 10 m/s. Calculate the centripetal force acting on the car.
questions.e: Centripetal force F = mv²/r = (800 x 10²)/50 = 800 x 100/50 = 1600 N. This force is directed towards the centre of the circular path and is provided by friction between the tyres and the road.
questions.p: Centripetal force na F = mv²/r = (800 x 10²)/50 = 800 x 100/50 = 1600 N. Na dis force dey point go centre of the circle, and na friction between tyre and road dey provide am.

questions.q: A stone is projected with a speed of 30 m/s at an angle of 60° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the maximum height reached by the stone.
questions.e: Maximum height H = u² sin²(theta)/(2g) = (30²)(sin60)²/20 = 900 x 0.75/20 = 33.75 m. Only the vertical component of the velocity (u sin theta) is used for the height calculation.
questions.p: Maximum height na H = u² sin²(theta)/(2g) = (30²)(sin60)²/20 = 900 x 0.75/20 = 33.75 m. Na only the up-down part of the speed (u sin theta) dem dey use calculate the height.

questions.q: A bucket containing water is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 1.0 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the minimum speed of the bucket at the topmost point of the circle so that the water does not spill out.
questions.e: At the top of the circle, for water not to spill, the weight of the water must supply just enough centripetal force: mg = mv²/r, so v = √gr = √(10 x 1.0) = √10 = 3.16 m/s. Below this speed, gravity would be more than needed, and the water would fall out before completing the loop.
questions.p: For top of the circle, make water no comot, the weight of water must jus provide the centripetal force wey e need: mg = mv²/r, so v = √gr = √(10 x 1.0) = √10 = 3.16 m/s. If speed too small pass dis, gravity go pull the water comot before e complete the loop.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines gravitational field intensity (gravitational field strength) at a point?
o: The force experienced per unit mass placed at that point
The force experienced per unit area at that point
The force experienced per unit charge placed at that point
The energy stored per unit mass at that point
questions.e: Gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force acting on a unit mass placed at a point in the field. It is measured in N/kg, which also equals m/s².
questions.p: Gravitational field strength na the force wey dey act on one kilogram mass for that point. E dey measured for N/kg, wey be same as m/s².

questions.q: A boy's school bag has a mass of 60 kg (including books) and weighs W on the Earth's surface, where g = 10 m/s². If the bag is taken to a height above the Earth's surface where the gravitational field strength reduces to one-quarter of its surface value, what is the new weight of the bag?
questions.e: Weight on Earth's surface = mg = 60 x 10 = 600 N. At the height given, g becomes 10/4 = 2.5 m/s², so new weight = 60 x 2.5 = 150 N.
questions.p: For surface, weight = mg = 60 x 10 = 600 N. For that height, g don reduce to 2.5 m/s², so new weight = 60 x 2.5 = 150 N.

questions.q: A simple pendulum has a length of 4 m. Taking g as pi² m/s², calculate the period of oscillation of the pendulum.
questions.e: T = 2pi × √(l/g) = 2pi × √(4/pi²) = 2pi × (2/π) = 4 s. The π cancels neatly because g was given as pi² m/s².
questions.p: T = 2pi × √(l/g) = 2pi × √(4/pi²) = 2pi × (2/π) = 4 s. The π cancel well-well because dem give g as pi² m/s².

questions.q: In simple harmonic motion, what is meant by the 'amplitude' of the motion?
o: The maximum displacement of the oscillating body from its mean (rest) position
The distance between two successive points moving in phase
The number of oscillations made per second
The time taken for one complete oscillation
questions.e: Amplitude is the greatest distance the oscillating body moves away from its equilibrium (mean) position during simple harmonic motion.
questions.p: Amplitude na the biggest distance wey the body waka comot from im resting position when e dey oscillate.

questions.q: A particle performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 5 cm and angular frequency 2 rad/s. Using v = omega × √(A² - x²), calculate the speed of the particle when its displacement from the mean position is 3 cm.

A simple pendulum has a period T when swinging on the Earth's surface, where the gravitational field strength is 10 m/s². If the same pendulum (same length) is taken to a planet where the gravitational field strength is 2.5 m/s², what is the new period in terms of T?
questions.e: Since T is proportional to 1/√g, the ratio of new period to old period is √(g_earth/g_planet) = √(10/2.5) = √4 = 2. So the new period is 2T; a weaker gravitational field makes the pendulum swing more slowly.
questions.p: T dey proportional to 1/√g, so new period divide old period give √(10/2.5) = √4 = 2. So new period na 2T; weak gravity make the pendulum swing slow-slow.

questions.q: A block of wood has a mass of 450 g and a volume of 500 cm³. What is the density of the wood in kg/m³?
questions.e: Density = mass/volume = 450 g / 500 cm³ = 0.9 g/cm³. Converting to kg/m³, multiply by 1000, giving 900 kg/m³.
questions.p: Density na mass divide by volume = 450g/500cm³ = 0.9 g/cm³. If you change am to kg/m³, you go multiply by 1000, e go be 900 kg/m³.

questions.q: A tank in Mrs. Okafor's shop contains water (density 1000 kg/m³) up to a depth of 2.5 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the pressure exerted by the water at the bottom of the tank.
questions.e: Pressure in a liquid is P = h x density x g = 2.5 x 1000 x 10 = 25000 N/m². This is the correct application of the liquid pressure formula.
questions.p: Pressure for liquid na P = h x density x g = 2.5 x 1000 x 10 = 25000 N/m². Na dis formula dem dey use calculate am.

questions.q: A stone weighs 8 N in air. When it is fully lowered into a beaker of water, it weighs 5 N. What is the upthrust on the stone?
questions.e: Upthrust is the loss in weight when an object is immersed in a liquid, so Upthrust = Weight in air - Weight in water = 8 N - 5 N = 3 N.
questions.p: Upthrust na di weight wey di stone lose for water, so Upthrust = Weight for air - Weight for water = 8N - 5N = 3N.

questions.q: A metal object of volume 200 cm³ is completely submerged in a liquid of density 1.25 g/cm³. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the upthrust on the object.
questions.e: Mass of liquid displaced = density x volume = 1.25 g/cm³ x 200 cm³ = 250 g = 0.25 kg. By Archimedes' principle, Upthrust = mg = 0.25 kg x 10 m/s² = 2.5 N.
questions.p: Mass of liquid wey e push comot = density x volume = 1.25 x 200 = 250 g = 0.25 kg. Upthrust = mg = 0.25 x 10 = 2.5 N, na so Archimedes principle take work.

questions.q: A block of plastic floats on water with 3/5 of its volume submerged. If the density of water is 1000 kg/m³, what is the density of the plastic block?
questions.e: For a floating body, the fraction submerged equals the ratio of the body's density to the liquid's density: fraction = density of object / density of liquid. So density of plastic = (3/5) x 1000 = 600 kg/m³.
questions.p: For floating object, di fraction wey dey inside liquid = density of object / density of liquid. So density of di plastic = (3/5) x 1000 = 600 kg/m³.

questions.q: Which law in Physics states that a floating body displaces a weight of fluid exactly equal to its own weight?
questions.e: The law of flotation states that a floating object displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats, which is why ships made of steel can float even though steel itself is denser than water.
questions.p: Law of flotation talk say any floating object go push comot liquid wey weight equal to im own weight, na why big steel ship fit float for water sef.

questions.q: The normal human body temperature is 37°C. What is this temperature on the Kelvin scale?
questions.e: To change Celsius to Kelvin, add 273. So 37°C + 273 = 310 K.
questions.p: To change from Celsius go Kelvin, you go add 273. So 37°C + 273 = 310 K.

questions.q: Mercury is commonly used in liquid-in-glass thermometers mainly because of which property?
o: It expands uniformly over a wide range of temperature
It freezes at a very high temperature
It has a very high specific heat capacity
It is a poor conductor of heat
questions.e: A good thermometric liquid must expand evenly as temperature rises so that equal temperature changes give equal changes in length (uniform scale). Mercury does this very well over a wide range.
questions.p: Good liquid wey dem go use for thermometer must expand well-well as the temperature dey rise, so that the scale go balance. Mercury dey do this one well for plenty temperature range.

questions.q: A steel rod of length 2 m is at a temperature of 20°C. If the linear expansivity of steel is 1.2 x 10⁻⁵ per K, calculate the increase in the length of the rod when it is heated to 120°C.
questions.e: Use ΔL = L x alpha x ΔT. Here ΔT = 120 - 20 = 100 K, so ΔL = 2 x 1.2x10⁻⁵ x 100 = 0.0024 m = 2.4 mm.
questions.p: Use ΔL = L x alpha x ΔT. ΔT = 120 - 20 = 100 K, so ΔL = 2 x 1.2x10⁻⁵ x 100 = 0.0024 m, wey be 2.4 mm.

questions.q: A bimetallic strip is made by firmly joining a brass strip and an iron strip together along their length, with brass expanding more than iron for the same rise in temperature. When the strip is heated evenly, which way does it bend?
o: It bends towards the brass side
It bends towards the iron side
questions.e: Since brass expands more than iron for the same temperature rise, the brass side becomes longer than the iron side. This forces the strip to curve, with the brass on the outside of the curve, so the strip bends towards the iron (the metal that expanded less).
questions.p: Since brass dey expand pass iron for the same temperature rise, the brass side go longer pass the iron side. This one go make the strip curve, brass go dey outside the curve, so the strip go bend go the iron side (the one wey expand less).

questions.q: A liquid has a real (absolute) cubical expansivity of 1.8 x 10⁻⁴ per K. When it is heated inside a glass container, the glass itself has a cubical expansivity of 2.7 x 10⁻⁵ per K. What is the apparent cubical expansivity of the liquid as observed in the glass container?
questions.e: Apparent expansivity = Real expansivity of liquid - cubical expansivity of container, because the container also expands and makes the liquid's level rise less than it really should. So apparent = 1.8x10⁻⁴ - 2.7x10⁻⁵ = 1.53x10⁻⁴ per K.
questions.p: Apparent expansivity = Real expansivity of the liquid minus the cubical expansivity of the container, because the container sef dey expand small, e dey reduce wetin we see. So apparent = 1.8x10⁻⁴ - 2.7x10⁻⁵ = 1.53x10⁻⁴ per K.

questions.q: A mercury-in-glass thermometer was wrongly calibrated so that the lower fixed point reads 2°C instead of 0°C, and the upper fixed point reads 102°C instead of 100°C. When this faulty thermometer is dipped into a liquid, it shows a reading of 56°C. What is the true temperature of the liquid?
questions.e: True temperature = [(observed reading - lower fixed point reading) / (upper fixed point reading - lower fixed point reading)] x 100. So True temp = (56 - 2)/(102 - 2) x 100 = 54/100 x 100 = 54°C.
questions.p: True temperature = [(wetin thermometer show - the lower fixed point reading) divide by (upper fixed point reading minus lower fixed point reading)] x 100. So True temp = (56 - 2)/(102 - 2) x 100 = 54/100 x 100 = 54°C.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines the heat capacity of a body?
o: the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of the whole body by 1 K
the quantity of heat needed to melt 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature
the quantity of heat lost per second by a hot body
the quantity of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K
questions.e: Heat capacity is the total quantity of heat needed to raise the temperature of a particular body (not per kg) by 1 K. It depends on the mass and specific heat capacity of the whole body.
questions.p: Heat capacity na di total heat wey dem need to raise di temperature of di whole body (not per kg) by 1 K. E depend on di mass and specific heat capacity of di body.

questions.q: A block of metal has a mass of 2 kg and specific heat capacity of 400 J/kgK. Calculate the heat capacity of the block.
questions.e: Heat capacity C = mass x specific heat capacity = 2 kg x 400 J/kgK = 800 J/K.
questions.p: Heat capacity C = mass x specific heat capacity = 2 kg x 400 J/kgK = 800 J/K.

questions.q: A kettle contains 3 kg of water at 25°C. Calculate the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of the water to 85°C. [Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kgK]
questions.e: Heat required Q = mcΔθ = 3 x 4200 x (85-25) = 3 x 4200 x 60 = 756000 J.
questions.p: Heat wey dem need Q = mcΔθ = 3 x 4200 x (85-25) = 3 x 4200 x 60 = 756000 J.

questions.q: Calculate the quantity of heat required to melt 0.5 kg of ice completely at its melting point. [Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334,000 J/kg]
questions.e: Heat needed Q = mL = 0.5 x 334000 = 167000 J. This heat changes the state of the ice without changing its temperature.
questions.p: Heat wey dem need Q = mL = 0.5 x 334000 = 167000 J. Dis heat dey change di state of di ice but e no dey change di temperature.

questions.q: A 2 kg block of ice at -5°C is to be completely converted to water at 15°C. Using specific heat capacity of ice = 2100 J/kgK, specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 334,000 J/kg, and specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kgK, calculate the total quantity of heat required.
questions.e: Three stages: (1) warm ice from -5°C to 0°C: 2x2100x5 = 21000 J. (2) melt ice at 0°C: 2x334000 = 668000 J. (3) warm water from 0°C to 15°C: 2x4200x15 = 126000 J. Total = 21000+668000+126000 = 815000 J.
questions.p: E get three stages: (1) warm di ice from -5°C to 0°C: 2x2100x5 = 21000 J. (2) melt di ice for 0°C: 2x334000 = 668000 J. (3) warm di water from 0°C to 15°C: 2x4200x15 = 126000 J. If you add dem, total na 815000 J.

questions.q: A metal block of heat capacity 200 J/K at 80°C is dropped into a liquid of heat capacity 800 J/K at 20°C inside a well-lagged container. Assuming no heat is lost to the surroundings, calculate the final common temperature of the mixture.
questions.e: Heat lost by metal = heat gained by liquid: 200(80-T) = 800(T-20). Expanding gives 16000-200T = 800T-16000, so 32000 = 1000T, giving T = 32°C.
questions.p: Heat wey metal lose = heat wey liquid gain: 200(80-T) = 800(T-20). If you expand am: 16000-200T = 800T-16000, so 32000=1000T, T=32°C.

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas occupies 400 cm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. If the temperature is kept constant and the pressure is increased to 200 kPa, what is the new volume of the gas?
questions.e: By Boyle's law, P1V1 = P2V2 at constant temperature. So 100 x 400 = 200 x V2, giving V2 = 200 cm³. The volume reduces because pressure has doubled.
questions.p: Boyle law talk say P1V1 = P2V2 if temperature no change. So 100 x 400 = 200 x V2, V2 go be 200 cm³. Volume reduce because pressure don double.

questions.q: A balloon contains gas with a volume of 300 cm³ at a temperature of 27°C. If the pressure is kept constant and the temperature is raised to 127°C, what is the new volume of the gas?
questions.e: Convert to Kelvin: T1 = 27+273 = 300K, T2 = 127+273 = 400K. By Charles' law, V1/T1 = V2/T2, so V2 = 300 x 400/300 = 400 cm³.
questions.p: Change the temperature go Kelvin: T1 = 300K, T2 = 400K. Charles law say V1/T1 = V2/T2, so V2 = 300 x 400/300 = 400 cm³.

questions.q: A sealed gas cylinder has a pressure of 2 atm at a temperature of 300K. If the volume is kept constant and the temperature rises to 450K, what will the new pressure be?
questions.e: By the pressure law (Gay-Lussac's law), P1/T1 = P2/T2 at constant volume. So P2 = 2 x 450/300 = 3 atm. Pressure rises because the gas molecules move faster and hit the walls harder.
questions.p: Pressure law (Gay-Lussac law) talk say P1/T1 = P2/T2 if volume no change. P2 = 2 x 450/300 = 3 atm. Pressure rise because the molecules dey move fast well well and dey hit the wall hard.

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 600 cm³ at a pressure of 150 kPa and a temperature of 300K. If the pressure changes to 100 kPa and the temperature changes to 350K, what is the new volume of the gas?
questions.e: Using the combined gas law, P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2. So V2 = (P1 x V1 x T2)/(T1 x P2) = (150 x 600 x 350)/(300 x 100) = 1050 cm³.
questions.p: Use the combined gas law: P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2. V2 = (150 x 600 x 350)/(300 x 100) = 1050 cm³.

questions.q: According to the kinetic theory of gases, why does the pressure of a fixed mass of gas in a closed, rigid container increase when the gas is heated?
o: The molecules increase in size as they absorb heat
The number of gas molecules in the container increases
The molecules move slower and collide with the walls less often
The molecules move faster, hit the walls more often and with greater force
questions.e: Heating a gas increases the average kinetic energy of its molecules, making them move faster. Faster molecules collide with the container walls more frequently and with greater force, which increases the pressure.
questions.p: If you heat gas, e go increase the kinetic energy of the molecules make dem move fast. The fast molecules go dey hit the wall more times and with more force, so pressure go increase.

questions.q: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 250 cm³ at a temperature of 17°C. If the pressure is kept constant, at what temperature (in °C) will the volume become 500 cm³?
questions.e: First convert 17°C to Kelvin: T1 = 17+273 = 290K. By Charles' law, V1/T1 = V2/T2, so T2 = 500 x 290/250 = 580K. Converting back to Celsius: 580 - 273 = 307°C.
questions.p: First change 17°C go Kelvin: T1 = 290K. Charles law: V1/T1 = V2/T2, so T2 = 500 x 290/250 = 580K. Change am back to Celsius: 580 - 273 = 307°C.

questions.q: Which of the following waves is best described as a longitudinal wave?
questions.e: In a longitudinal wave, the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth in the same direction as the wave travels, as happens with sound waves in air. Light, water and radio waves are transverse waves.
questions.p: Sound wave na longitudinal wave because the air particles dey vibrate for the same direction wey the wave dey move go. Light, water and radio waves be transverse wave, so dem no fit be the answer.

questions.q: In a transverse wave travelling along a rope, the distance between two successive crests is called the wave's:
questions.e: Wavelength is defined as the distance between two successive points that are in the same phase, such as crest to crest or trough to trough. Amplitude is the maximum displacement, frequency is the number of waves per second, and period is the time for one complete wave.
questions.p: Wavelength na the distance between two crest wey dey follow each other for the wave. Amplitude na the highest point from the middle line, frequency na how many wave dey pass per second, period na the time for one complete wave.

questions.q: A sound wave produced by a loudspeaker at a market in Onitsha has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 4 m. Calculate the speed of the wave.
questions.e: Wave speed is found using v = f x wavelength. So v = 50 Hz x 4 m = 200 m/s.
questions.p: To find wave speed, we use v = f x wavelength. So v = 50 x 4 = 200 m/s.

questions.q: A vibrating string completes 20 full oscillations in 4 seconds. Calculate the period of the oscillation.
questions.e: Period is the time taken for one complete oscillation, found by dividing total time by number of oscillations. T = 4 s / 20 = 0.2 s.
questions.p: Period na the time wey one complete oscillation take. T = total time divide by number of oscillation = 4/20 = 0.2 s.

questions.q: A wave of frequency 250 Hz and wavelength 1.2 m is travelling in medium X. It then enters medium Y, where its speed reduces to three-quarters of its original speed, while the frequency stays the same. Calculate the new wavelength of the wave in medium Y.
questions.e: First find the original speed: v = f x wavelength = 250 x 1.2 = 300 m/s. The new speed in medium Y is 3/4 of 300 = 225 m/s. Since frequency is unchanged, new wavelength = new speed / frequency = 225 / 250 = 0.9 m.
questions.p: First find the original speed: v = f x wavelength = 250 x 1.2 = 300 m/s. The new speed for medium Y na 3/4 of 300 = 225 m/s. Since the frequency no change, new wavelength = 225/250 = 0.9 m.

questions.q: Which property of waves best explains why a person standing near a tall wall hears an echo of their own shout?
questions.e: An echo occurs when sound waves bounce back from a hard surface such as a wall, which is an example of reflection. Refraction is bending due to change in speed, diffraction is spreading around obstacles, and polarisation applies only to transverse waves restricting vibration to one plane.
questions.p: Echo dey happen when sound wave bounce back from hard surface like wall, and that na reflection. Refraction na when wave bend because speed change, diffraction na when wave spread round obstacle, and polarisation na for transverse wave wey dem restrict make e vibrate for one plane only.

questions.q: The range of frequencies that a normal human ear can detect is approximately:
questions.e: The normal human ear can hear sounds with frequencies between 20 Hz and 20000 Hz. Sounds below 20 Hz are infrasonic and those above 20000 Hz are ultrasonic, both inaudible to humans.
questions.p: Normal human ear fit hear sound wey dey between 20 Hz to 20000 Hz. Anything wey dey below 20 Hz na infrasound, anything above 20000 Hz na ultrasound, man no fit hear am.

questions.q: Sound waves are best classified as which type of wave?
questions.e: Sound waves travel by compressions and rarefactions, with particles vibrating parallel to the direction of wave travel. This makes sound a longitudinal wave, unlike light which is transverse.
questions.p: Sound dey waka through compression and rarefaction, and the particles dey vibrate for the same direction wey the wave dey go. Na why we dey call am longitudinal wave, e no be like light wey be transverse.

questions.q: Chidinma stands 170 m away from a tall wall at Yankari National Park. She claps once and hears the echo exactly 1.0 second later. Calculate the speed of sound in air.
questions.e: The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total distance is 2 x 170 m = 340 m. Speed = distance/time = 340 m / 1.0 s = 340 m/s.
questions.p: The sound go reach wall come back, so the total distance na 2 x 170 m = 340 m. Speed = distance/time = 340 m / 1.0 s = 340 m/s.

questions.q: A tuning fork produces a sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travelling through air at a speed of 340 m/s. Calculate the wavelength of the sound wave.
questions.e: Wavelength = speed/frequency = 340 m/s divided by 500 Hz = 0.68 m. This uses the wave equation v = f x wavelength rearranged to find wavelength.
questions.p: Wavelength = speed/frequency = 340 m/s divide by 500 Hz = 0.68 m. Na the wave formula v = f x wavelength wey we just rearrange.

questions.q: Two tuning forks are sounded together, one with frequency 256 Hz and the other with frequency 260 Hz. How many beats per second will a listener hear?
questions.e: The number of beats per second equals the difference between the two frequencies. So beats = 260 Hz - 256 Hz = 4 beats per second, heard as a throbbing rise and fall in loudness.
questions.p: Number of beats per second na the difference between the two frequencies. So beats = 260 Hz - 256 Hz = 4 beats per second, wey person go hear as the sound dey rise and fall for loudness.

questions.q: The speed of sound in air at 0°C is 332 m/s. If the speed increases by 0.6 m/s for every 1°C rise in temperature, calculate the speed of sound in air at 30°C.
questions.e: Increase in speed = 0.6 m/s x 30 = 18 m/s. New speed = 332 m/s + 18 m/s = 350 m/s. This shows that speed of sound increases as air temperature rises.
questions.p: Increase for speed = 0.6 m/s x 30 = 18 m/s. New speed = 332 m/s + 18 m/s = 350 m/s. E dey show say as temperature dey rise, sound speed dey rise too.

questions.q: A student standing in front of a plane mirror in Kaduna observes her image. Which of the following is NOT a correct property of the image formed by a plane mirror?
o: It is the same size as the object
It is diminished (smaller than the object)
questions.e: A plane mirror always forms an image that is the same size as the object, so it cannot be diminished. The image is virtual and laterally inverted, but never smaller or larger than the object.
questions.p: Plane mirror dey always give image wey match the object size, e no fit be smaller pass am. Dat image na virtual and e dey laterally flip, but e no dey shrink.

questions.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror making an angle of 35° with the surface of the mirror (not the normal). What is the angle of reflection?
questions.e: The angle given is measured from the mirror surface, so the angle of incidence (from the normal) is 90° - 35° = 55°. By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, which is 55°.
questions.p: Dem give angle from the mirror surface, so to find the one wey dey from normal, we do 90° - 35° = 55°. Law of reflection talk say angle of reflection go equal angle of incidence, so e remain 55°.

questions.q: Two plane mirrors are arranged so that they are inclined to each other at an angle of 60°. An object, a small coin, is placed between them. How many images of the coin will be formed?
questions.e: For two inclined mirrors, the number of images formed is given by (360/angle) - 1. Using 360/60 - 1 = 6 - 1 = 5, five images are formed.
questions.p: When mirror two dey lean for each other, number of images na (360 divide by the angle) minus 1. 360/60 give 6, minus 1 na 5 images.

questions.q: A concave mirror used in a torchlight reflector has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. What is the focal length of this mirror?
questions.e: For a curved mirror, the focal length is half the radius of curvature, so f = R/2. With R = 40 cm, f = 40/2 = 20 cm.
questions.p: For curve mirror, focal length na half of the radius of curvature, so f = R/2. R be 40 cm, so f = 40/2 = 20 cm.

questions.q: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror, and a real image is formed 30 cm from the mirror on the same side. Using the mirror formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, calculate the focal length of the mirror.
questions.e: Using 1/f = 1/u + 1/v = 1/15 + 1/30 = 2/30 + 1/30 = 3/30 = 1/10, so f = 10 cm. This shows the focal length is less than both the object and image distances, as expected for a concave mirror producing a real image.
questions.p: We take 1/f = 1/15 + 1/30 = 2/30 + 1/30 = 3/30 = 1/10, so f = 10 cm. Dis one show say focal length small pass both object and image distance, wey correct for concave mirror wey form real image.

questions.q: An object of height 2 cm is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror whose focal length is 10 cm. Using the mirror formula and magnification relation (m = v/u = image height/object height), find the height of the image formed.
questions.e: From the mirror formula, 1/f = 1/u + 1/v gives 1/10 = 1/20 + 1/v, so 1/v = 1/20, meaning v = 20 cm. The magnification m = v/u = 20/20 = 1, so the image height equals the object height, which is 2 cm (the image is real and inverted but same size).
questions.p: From mirror formula, 1/10 = 1/20 + 1/v, so 1/v = 1/20, meaning v = 20 cm. Magnification m = v/u = 20/20 = 1, so image height go match object height wey be 2 cm (image real and e flip, but size no change).

questions.q: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block of refractive index 1.5. If the angle of incidence is 30°, calculate the angle of refraction. (sin 30° = 0.5)
questions.e: Using n = sin i / sin r, we get sin r = sin i / n = 0.5 / 1.5 = 0.333. Taking the inverse sine gives r = 19.5°.
questions.p: Dem use n = sin i / sin r, so sin r = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333. If you find inverse sine of 0.333, you go get r = 19.5°.

questions.q: A converging (convex) lens has a focal length of 10 cm. An object is placed 15 cm from the lens. Using the lens formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, calculate the distance of the image from the lens.
questions.e: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/10 - 1/15 = (3-2)/30 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm. This means the image forms 30 cm from the lens.
questions.p: 1/v = 1/10 - 1/15 = 1/30, so v = 30 cm. Na so the image dey form 30 cm from the lens.

questions.q: A convex lens forms a real, inverted image 6 cm high from an object that is 2 cm high. Calculate the linear magnification produced by the lens.
questions.e: Linear magnification, m = image height / object height = 6/2 = 3. This tells us the image is 3 times bigger than the object.
questions.p: Magnification, m = image height divide object height = 6/2 = 3. E mean say the image big pass the object by 3 times.

questions.q: The refractive index of a certain type of glass is 1.5. Calculate the critical angle for light travelling from the glass into air. (sin C = 1/n)
questions.e: sin C = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667. Taking the inverse sine of 0.667 gives C = 41.8°, which is the critical angle for total internal reflection to just occur.
questions.p: sin C = 1/1.5 = 0.667. If you find inverse sine, you go get C = 41.8°, na so total internal reflection go just begin.

questions.q: In a compound microscope, which of the following best describes the function of the objective lens?
o: It bends light rays from distant objects so they appear closer, like in a telescope
It forms a real, inverted and magnified image of the object close to the eyepiece
It magnifies the final image formed by the eyepiece for direct viewing
It reduces the size of the object so it can fit into the eyepiece
questions.e: The objective lens, which is closest to the object, forms a real, inverted and magnified image near the eyepiece; the eyepiece then further magnifies this image for the eye to view. The other options describe the eyepiece or unrelated functions.
questions.p: The objective lens wey dey close to the object go form real, upside-down and bigger image near the eyepiece; na the eyepiece go then magnify am more for eye to see. The other options na the eyepiece work or no relate at all.

questions.q: A glass rod is rubbed with a piece of silk cloth. After rubbing, the glass rod is found to carry a positive charge while the silk becomes negatively charged. Which statement correctly explains this observation?
o: Electrons are transferred from the silk to the glass rod, giving the glass rod extra electrons
Electrons are transferred from the glass rod to the silk, leaving the glass rod with a deficit of electrons
Protons move from the silk cloth onto the glass rod
The glass rod absorbs extra electrons from the surrounding air during rubbing
questions.e: When glass and silk are rubbed together, silk holds electrons more strongly than glass, so electrons move from the glass to the silk. This leaves the glass rod with fewer electrons than protons, making it positively charged.
questions.p: When you rub glass rod with silk, silk get more power to hold electron pass glass, so electron dey waka comot from glass go silk. Dis one make glass get less electron pass proton, so e become positive.

questions.q: What is the SI unit used to measure the capacitance of a capacitor?
questions.e: Capacitance tells us how much charge a capacitor can store per volt applied across it, and this quantity is measured in farads (F). Coulomb measures charge, volt measures potential difference, and ohm measures resistance.
questions.p: Capacitance na how much charge one capacitor fit hold for every volt wey dem apply am. Dem dey measure am for farad, no be coulomb, volt or ohm.

questions.q: A capacitor of 4 microfarads and another of 12 microfarads are connected in series across a battery. What is the effective (equivalent) capacitance of the combination?
questions.e: For capacitors in series, 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 = 1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3, so C = 3 microfarads. Note that series combination always gives a value smaller than the smallest individual capacitor.
questions.p: For capacitor wey dem connect for series, 1/C = 1/4 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3, so C = 3 microfarad. Series combination go always small pass di smallest capacitor wey dey inside am.

questions.q: Three capacitors of capacitance 2 microfarads, 3 microfarads and 5 microfarads are connected in parallel to a 12 V battery. What is the total (equivalent) capacitance of the arrangement?
questions.e: For capacitors connected in parallel, the equivalent capacitance is simply the sum of the individual capacitances: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 microfarads. Parallel combination always gives a value larger than the largest individual capacitor.
questions.p: For capacitor wey dem connect for parallel, you just add dem together: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 microfarad. Parallel combination go always big pass di biggest capacitor wey dey inside am.

questions.q: A capacitor of capacitance 5 microfarads is charged until the potential difference across its plates is 200 V. Calculate the energy stored in the capacitor.
questions.e: Energy stored, E = (1/2)CV² = 0.5 x 5x10⁻⁶ x 200² = 0.5 x 5x10⁻⁶ x 40000 = 0.1 J. A common mistake is leaving out the factor of 1/2, which doubles the answer to 0.2 J.
questions.p: Energy wey capacitor store, E = (1/2)CV² = 0.5 x 5x10⁻⁶ x 200² = 0.1 J. People wey forget di 1/2 go mistakenly carry 0.2 J as answer.

questions.q: Two point charges of magnitude 2 x 10⁻⁶ C and 3 x 10⁻⁶ C are placed 0.3 m apart in air. Using Coulomb's constant k = 9 x 10⁹ Nm²/C², calculate the electrostatic force of repulsion between them.
questions.e: Using F = kq1q2/r² = (9x10⁹ x 2x10⁻⁶ x 3x10⁻⁶) / (0.3)² = (9x10⁹ x 6x10⁻¹²) / 0.09 = 0.054 / 0.09 = 0.6 N. Squaring the distance correctly is the key step many students miss.
questions.p: Use F = kq1q2/r² = (9x10⁹ x 2x10⁻⁶ x 3x10⁻⁶) / (0.3)² = 0.054 / 0.09 = 0.6 N. Di key step na to square di distance well-well before you divide.

questions.q: A wire has a resistance of 5 ohms. If a current of 2 A flows through it, what is the voltage across the wire?
questions.e: By Ohm's law, V = IR. So V = 2 A x 5 ohms = 10 V.
questions.p: Ohm's law talk say V = IR. So V = 2 A x 5 ohms = 10 V.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly states Ohm's law?
o: The resistance of a conductor increases as the voltage across it decreases, at constant temperature
The current through a conductor is inversely proportional to its resistance, regardless of temperature
The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it, provided temperature and other physical conditions remain constant
The voltage across a conductor is constant no matter the current flowing through it
questions.e: Ohm's law states that current is directly proportional to voltage when temperature and physical conditions are constant, giving V = IR. The other options either ignore the temperature condition or state a wrong relationship.
questions.p: Ohm's law talk say current dey proportional to voltage as long as temperature and other condition no change, so V = IR. The other options no follow this correct relationship.

questions.q: Three resistors of 2 ohms, 3 ohms and 5 ohms are connected in series to a battery of electromotive force 20 V. What is the current flowing in the circuit?
questions.e: In series, total resistance R = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 ohms. Using I = V/R, I = 20/10 = 2 A.
questions.p: For series, total resistance na R = 2+3+5 = 10 ohms. Then I = V/R = 20/10 = 2 A.

questions.q: An electric bulb is rated 60 W, 240 V. What current does it draw when working normally?
questions.e: Power P = VI, so I = P/V = 60/240 = 0.25 A. This is the normal operating current of the bulb.
questions.p: Power P = VI, so I = P/V = 60/240 = 0.25 A. Na so the bulb dey take draw current when e dey work well well.

questions.q: Two resistors of 4 ohms and 6 ohms are connected in parallel across a cell. What is their equivalent resistance?
questions.e: For parallel resistors, 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 = 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12, so R = 12/5 = 2.4 ohms.
questions.p: For parallel resistors, 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12, so R = 12/5 = 2.4 ohms.

questions.q: An electric heater is rated 1000 W. Mrs Adaeze uses it for 3 hours every day for 30 days. If the Power Holding Company charges ₦50 per kilowatt-hour, what is the total cost of energy used?
questions.e: Energy used = Power x Time = 1 kW x 3 h x 30 days = 90 kWh. Cost = 90 kWh x ₦50 = ₦4500.
questions.p: Energy wey dem use = 1 kW x 3 h x 30 days = 90 kWh. Cost = 90 kWh x ₦50 = ₦4500.

questions.q: Which of these materials is NOT attracted by a magnet?
questions.e: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic materials that are strongly attracted to a magnet. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, both of which are non-magnetic, so brass is not attracted.
questions.p: Iron, nickel and cobalt na magnetic materials wey magnet go pull well-well. Brass na mixture of copper and zinc, dem no be magnetic, so magnet no go pull am.

questions.q: An unmagnetized steel nail is held close to, but not touching, a strong bar magnet. After some time, the nail becomes magnetized even though it never touched the magnet. This process is called
questions.e: Magnetic induction is the process by which a magnetic material becomes magnetized simply by being placed near (not touching) a magnet, due to the magnet's field. Electromagnetic induction instead refers to producing an EMF/current from a changing magnetic field in a conductor.
questions.p: Magnetic induction na when magnetic material dey become magnet just because e dey near another magnet, even without touch am. Electromagnetic induction na different thing, e dey talk about EMF or current wey changing field dey produce for wire.

questions.q: A coil of 200 turns is placed in a magnetic field. The magnetic flux linking the coil changes from 0.02 Wb to 0.08 Wb in 0.3 seconds. Calculate the average EMF induced in the coil, using EMF = N x (change in flux)/(time).
questions.e: Change in flux = 0.08 - 0.02 = 0.06 Wb. EMF = N x (delta Phi / t) = 200 x (0.06/0.3) = 200 x 0.2 = 40V.
questions.p: Change in flux na 0.08 minus 0.02 = 0.06 Wb. EMF = N x (delta Phi divide t) = 200 x (0.06/0.3) = 200 x 0.2 = 40V.

questions.q: A bar magnet is pushed, north pole first, into a solenoid that is connected to a sensitive galvanometer. According to Lenz's law, the induced current that flows in the solenoid acts in a direction that
o: aids the motion of the magnet
has no effect on the magnet
moves at twice the magnet's speed
opposes the motion of the magnet
questions.e: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is always such that it opposes the change (the motion) that produced it. So the solenoid's induced current creates a magnetic field that pushes back against the incoming magnet, opposing its motion.
questions.p: Lenz's law talk say the induced current go always resist the motion wey cause am. So the solenoid go produce field wey dey push back the magnet, e no go help the magnet motion.

questions.q: A transformer has a primary coil of 1000 turns and a secondary coil of 100 turns. The primary is connected to a 240V supply and draws a current of 2A. Assuming the transformer is 100% efficient, calculate the current flowing in the secondary coil.
questions.e: First find secondary voltage: Vs = Vp x (Ns/Np) = 240 x (100/1000) = 24V. Since input power equals output power (100% efficient): Vp x Ip = Vs x Is, so Is = (240 x 2)/24 = 20A.
questions.p: First find Vs: Vs = Vp x (Ns/Np) = 240 x (100/1000) = 24V. Since input power equal output power (100% efficient): Vp x Ip = Vs x Is, so Is = (240 x 2)/24 = 20A.

questions.q: A straight metal rod of length 0.5m moves with a velocity of 4 m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.2T. Calculate the EMF induced across the ends of the rod, using EMF = B x L x v.
questions.e: EMF = B x L x v = 0.2 x 0.5 x 4 = 0.4V. The rod cutting across the field lines generates this motional EMF because it is moving perpendicular to the field.
questions.p: EMF = B x L x v = 0.2 x 0.5 x 4 = 0.4V. The rod wey dey cut the field lines go generate this EMF because e dey move perpendicular to the field.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the nature of an alpha particle emitted during radioactive decay?
o: A helium nucleus made up of 2 protons and 2 neutrons
A fast-moving electron with negative charge
A neutral particle with no mass and no charge
An electromagnetic wave with no mass and no charge
questions.e: An alpha particle is identical to the nucleus of a helium atom, containing 2 protons and 2 neutrons, giving it a charge of +2 and a mass number of 4. This makes it heavier and less penetrating than beta or gamma radiation.
questions.p: Alpha particle be like helium nucleus wey get 2 protons and 2 neutrons inside am. E get +2 charge and e no fit waka far pass paper or skin, unlike beta and gamma rays.

questions.q: In the study of radioactivity, the half-life of a radioactive substance is best defined as the time taken for:
o: all the atoms in the sample to decay completely
half of the radioactive atoms in the sample to decay
the mass of the sample to double in size
the radiation from the sample to disappear totally
questions.e: Half-life is a fixed, measurable period during which exactly half of the radioactive nuclei present in a sample decay into another element. It never refers to complete decay, since radioactive decay theoretically never reaches zero.
questions.p: Half-life na the time wey half of the radioactive atoms inside sample go don decay finish. E no mean say everything go finish decay, na only half.

questions.q: Three types of radiation - alpha, beta and gamma - are compared for their ability to pass through a thick sheet of lead. Which type of radiation has the greatest penetrating power and can pass through several centimetres of lead?
questions.e: Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves with no mass or charge, which allows them to penetrate deeply through dense materials like lead. Alpha particles are stopped by paper, while beta particles are stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
questions.p: Gamma rays no get mass or charge, na pure energy wave, so e fit waka pass thick lead sheet. Alpha dey stop by paper, beta dey stop by small aluminium sheet.

questions.q: A radioactive isotope decays such that only 1/8 of the original number of atoms remains after 24 hours. What is the half-life of the isotope?
questions.e: 1/8 equals (1/2)³, so 3 half-lives have passed in 24 hours. Dividing 24 hours by 3 gives a half-life of 8 hours. Checking: after 8 hrs, 1/2 remains; after 16 hrs, 1/4; after 24 hrs, 1/8 remains, which matches the question.
questions.p: 1/8 na (1/2) raise to 3, so na 3 half-lives dey inside the 24 hours. 24 divide by 3 give 8 hours as half-life. If you check: 8hrs=1/2, 16hrs=1/4, 24hrs=1/8, e correct.

questions.q: A radioactive nuclide X has a mass number of 238 and an atomic number of 92. It emits a single alpha particle to form a new nuclide Y. What are the mass number and atomic number of Y respectively?
questions.e: An alpha particle has a mass number of 4 and atomic number of 2. So the new mass number is 238 - 4 = 234, and the new atomic number is 92 - 2 = 90. This matches the pattern for alpha decay in nuclear equations.
questions.p: Alpha particle get mass number 4 and atomic number 2. So new mass number na 238 minus 4 = 234, and new atomic number na 92 minus 2 = 90. Na so alpha decay dey work for nuclear equation.

questions.q: Which pair of elements below are the semiconductor materials most commonly used in manufacturing diodes and transistors?
questions.e: Silicon and Germanium have four valence electrons and their conductivity lies between that of conductors and insulators, making them ideal for doping to produce diodes and transistors. Copper, Aluminium, Iron and Nickel are good conductors, not semiconductors.
questions.p: Silicon and Germanium na the semiconductor materials wey dem dey use make diode and transistor because dem get four valence electrons. Copper, Aluminium, Iron and Nickel na conductors, dem no be semiconductor.

questions.q: A pure (intrinsic) silicon crystal is doped with a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus, which has five valence electrons. What type of semiconductor is formed?
questions.e: A pentavalent impurity (5 valence electrons) donates an extra free electron to the silicon lattice, increasing the number of free negative charge carriers. This produces an n-type semiconductor, where electrons are the majority carriers.
questions.p: Pentavalent impurity like phosphorus get five valence electrons, so e dey give extra free electron to the silicon. This one dey make n-type semiconductor, where electron na the majority carrier.

questions.q: A p-n junction diode is connected in forward bias, meaning the positive terminal of the battery is joined to the p-type side and the negative terminal to the n-type side. What happens to the depletion region and the current flow?
o: The depletion region narrows and current flows easily
The depletion region widens and no current flows
The depletion region stays unchanged and current flows in reverse
The depletion region widens and current flows easily
questions.e: In forward bias, the applied voltage pushes majority carriers toward the junction, which reduces (narrows) the depletion region and allows current to flow easily through the diode. In reverse bias the opposite happens, the depletion region widens and current is blocked.
questions.p: For forward bias, the voltage dey push the majority carriers go the junction, so the depletion region dey narrow and current dey waka well well. If na reverse bias, depletion region go widen and current no go flow.

questions.q: In an electronic circuit used to charge a phone battery, a junction diode is included mainly to:
o: Convert alternating current into direct current
questions.e: A junction diode only allows current to flow in one direction (forward bias) and blocks it in the other (reverse bias). This property is used for rectification, converting AC from the mains into DC needed to charge the battery.
questions.p: Diode dey only allow current to flow for one direction and e dey block am for the other direction. Na so e dey rectify AC come DC wey dem dey use charge phone battery.

questions.q: A simple half-wave rectifier circuit is connected to an alternating current supply of frequency 50 Hz. What is the frequency of the rectified (output) voltage pulses produced by the circuit?
questions.e: A half-wave rectifier allows only one half of each AC cycle to pass through, producing one output pulse for every complete input cycle. Therefore the output frequency equals the input frequency, which is 50 Hz.
questions.p: Half-wave rectifier dey allow only one half of the AC cycle pass, so na one pulse e dey give for every complete cycle. That means the output frequency go still be 50 Hz, same as the input.

questions.q: A full-wave bridge rectifier made of four diodes is connected to an alternating current mains supply of frequency 60 Hz. What is the frequency of the output pulses produced by this rectifier?
questions.e: A full-wave bridge rectifier uses both halves (positive and negative) of each AC cycle, producing two output pulses for every one input cycle. So the output frequency is twice the supply frequency: 2 x 60 Hz = 120 Hz.
questions.p: Full-wave bridge rectifier dey use both the positive and negative half of the AC cycle, so e dey produce two pulses for every one cycle wey enter. That means output frequency na 2 x 60 Hz = 120 Hz.
